W3 — Polygenic Risk Scores (PRS)

Clinical Genomics for Bioinformatics

Author

Eunji Ha

Published

June 3, 2026

From GWAS hits to clinical risk

The limitation of single GWAS hits

From W2:

  • GWAS finds variants at p < 5×10⁻⁸
  • But most complex diseases are polygenic / omnigenic — thousands of variants
  • Each with a tiny effect (OR ≈ 1.02–1.15)
  • No single variant is clinically useful alone

A PRS aggregates the effects of (up to) millions of SNPs into one number per person.

What a PRS is

For person i, sum the GWAS effect size \(\hat\beta_j\) × allele dosage \(G_{ij}\) over all variants j:

\[\text{PRS}_i = \sum_{j=1}^{M} \hat\beta_j \, G_{ij}\]

Person A:
  rs1001  risk allele × 0.03
+ rs2045  risk allele × 0.02
+ rs8821  non-risk    × 0.00
+ ... (thousands–millions more)
─────────────────────────────────
= PRS 1.42  → top 20% of population → ~3× risk

Crucially, variants below genome-wide significance still carry real signal — PRS deliberately includes them [Reay & Cairns 2021].

Why it works: the omnigenic premise

  • W2’s omnigenic model: thousands of variants each nudge the trait
  • Single hits capture a sliver of heritability; aggregation captures much more
  • PRS is the clinical pay-off of polygenicity — one saliva sample → lifetime genetic predisposition
Note

A PRS is a risk indicator, not a diagnosis. It shifts a probability; it does not determine an outcome.

Where PRS is already being trialled

  • Coronary artery disease — flags high-risk people for earlier statins
  • Breast cancer — stratifies risk beyond BRCA1/2; guides screening intensity
  • Type 2 diabetes — PRS + lifestyle → targeted prevention
  • Atrial fibrillation — predicts incident AF beyond clinical scores
  • Prostate / colorectal cancer — screening intensity
TipThe clinician’s question

PRS adds information on top of age, BMI, family history, biomarkers. The bar is always: does it change management?

How a PRS is built

Method 1 — C+T (clumping + thresholding)

The simplest, most interpretable approach:

1. Clump  : keep one SNP per LD block (independent signals)
2. Threshold : keep SNPs below a p-value cutoff (e.g. 5e-8, 0.05, ...)
3. Score  : PRS = Σ (effect size × allele dosage)
library(bigsnpr)

obj.bigsnp <- snp_attach(here::here("data", "raw", "target.rds"))
G <- obj.bigsnp$genotypes

ind.keep <- snp_clumping(
  G,
  infos.chr = obj.bigsnp$map$chromosome,
  infos.pos = obj.bigsnp$map$physical.pos,
  S         = abs(sumstats$beta / sumstats$beta_se),  # rank by |Z|
  thr.r2    = 0.1,
  size      = 500
)
Warning

The p-value threshold is arbitrary — C+T discards sub-threshold signal and needs tuning on a validation set.

Method 2 — LDpred2 (Bayesian, current standard)

Models LD explicitly and reweights all variants (no hard cutoff) under a Bayesian prior [Reay & Cairns 2021].

# 1) Match summary stats to target
sumstats <- snp_match(sumstats, obj.bigsnp$map)

# 2) LD reference (genetic positions → correlation matrix)
POS2 <- snp_asGeneticPos(obj.bigsnp$map$chromosome,
                         obj.bigsnp$map$physical.pos,
                         dir = here::here("data", "raw", "genetic_maps"))
corr <- snp_cor(G, ind.col = sumstats$`_NUM_ID_`,
                infos.pos = POS2, size = 3 / 1000)

# 3) Estimate h2, then LDpred2-auto (no validation set needed)
ldsc <- with(sumstats, snp_ldsc(ld_score, ld_size = nrow(G),
                                chi2 = (beta / beta_se)^2, sample_size = n_eff))
multi_auto <- snp_ldpred2_auto(corr, sumstats, h2_init = ldsc[["h2"]],
                               vec_p_init = seq_log(1e-4, 0.2, 30),
                               burn_in = 500, num_iter = 500)

Method 3 — PRSice2 (practical workhorse)

# Command-line tool, called from R
system(paste(
  "PRSice",
  "--base",          here::here("data", "raw", "sumstats.txt"),
  "--target",        here::here("data", "raw", "target_plink"),
  "--binary-target", "T",
  "--pheno",         here::here("data", "raw", "phenotype.txt"),
  "--cov",           here::here("data", "raw", "covariates.txt"),
  "--out",           here::here("results", "prsice_output"),
  "--thread",        4
))
Note

PRSice2 auto-optimizes the p-value threshold and emits bar / high-resolution / quantile plots out of the box.

Choosing a method

Method Pros Cons
C+T fast, interpretable loses signal, arbitrary threshold
LDpred2 best accuracy, principled, -auto needs no tuning slower, needs LD reference
PRSice2 easy, great plots threshold-based
PRS-CS / PRS-CSx continuous shrinkage; multi-ancestry needs Python; LD panel

Clinical research: LDpred2 or PRSice2. Multi-ancestry: PRS-CSx. Consider a composite of several methods to reduce single-method assumptions [Kullo 2025].

Evaluating a PRS

Incremental variance (Nagelkerke R²)

Always report PRS performance above a clinical baseline — never PRS alone.

library(tidyverse); library(DescTools)

prs_data <- read_tsv(here::here("results", "prsice_output.best")) |>
  left_join(phenotype, by = "IID")

null_model <- glm(disease ~ age + sex + PC1+PC2+PC3+PC4+PC5,
                  data = prs_data, family = binomial)
full_model <- glm(disease ~ PRS + age + sex + PC1+PC2+PC3+PC4+PC5,
                  data = prs_data, family = binomial)

r2_prs <- PseudoR2(full_model, "Nagelkerke") -
          PseudoR2(null_model, "Nagelkerke")
cat("Incremental R² from PRS:", round(r2_prs, 4), "\n")

Discrimination (AUC)

library(pROC)

roc_null <- roc(prs_data$disease, predict(null_model, type = "response"))
roc_full <- roc(prs_data$disease, predict(full_model, type = "response"))

roc.test(roc_null, roc_full)   # does PRS add discrimination?

ggroc(list(Clinical = roc_null, `Clinical + PRS` = roc_full)) +
  labs(title = "Does PRS improve prediction?", color = "Model") +
  theme_minimal()
Note

A statistically significant AUC bump can still be clinically trivial. Pair AUC with reclassification (NRI) and, above all, calibration.

Calibration — the underappreciated metric

Calibration = do predicted probabilities match observed frequencies? [Kullo 2025]

  • Of people told “10% 10-year risk”, do ~10% develop disease?
  • A PRS well-calibrated in one population can be miscalibrated in another (different baseline risk, covariate distributions)
  • Fix by recalibration (update baseline hazard / intercept); assess in independent, population-representative cohorts
Important

Good discrimination ≠ good calibration. A model can rank people correctly yet output systematically wrong probabilities.

Quantile plot — the clinical view

prs_data <- prs_data |> mutate(prs_decile = ntile(PRS, 10))

or_by_decile <- prs_data |>
  group_by(prs_decile) |>
  summarise(n_cases = sum(disease == 1),
            n_ctrl  = sum(disease == 0), .groups = "drop") |>
  mutate(odds = n_cases / n_ctrl,
         OR   = odds / odds[prs_decile == 5])   # vs middle decile

ggplot(or_by_decile, aes(prs_decile, OR)) +
  geom_col(fill = "#185FA5") +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 1, linetype = "dashed") +
  labs(x = "PRS decile", y = "OR vs middle decile",
       title = "Disease risk by PRS decile") +
  theme_minimal()

Same disease, different PRS → different person flagged

  • Two PRSs with similar population AUC can disagree on which individual is high-risk [Kullo 2025]
  • Mitigations: consensus thresholds (high-risk only if top-tier across ≥2 scores) or a composite score
  • Risk also changes over time (age, comorbidity, exposures) → re-score with up-to-date methods; keep raw genotypes

Is it clinically useful? The ACCE lens

Four questions before the clinic (ACCE)

The 2025 review frames PRS readiness with the ACCE framework [Kullo 2025]:

  • Analytical validity — does the assay/pipeline measure the score accurately & reproducibly?
  • Clinical validity — does the score actually associate with the disease in the target population?
  • Clinical utility — does using it improve outcomes?
  • Ethical, legal, social implications — equity, consent, insurance, communication

Most PRSs clear analytical and clinical validity; the bottleneck is utility and ELSI.

Evidence for clinical utility is still thin

Few completed RCTs [Kullo 2025]:

  • MI-GENES (CHD) — PRS-integrated risk → lower LDL at 6 mo, fewer events at 10 yr (earlier/longer statin use)
  • GenoVA — PRS for 6 diseases (CHD, T2D, AF, breast/colorectal/prostate cancer): effect on time-to-diagnosis
  • WISDOM / PERSPECTIVE — PRS-guided mammography intensity
  • eMERGE (US, 10 conditions) and Our Future Health (UK, 5M) — implementation at scale
Note

RCTs are slow and costly — cohort, health-economics, simulation and implementation-science studies all contribute evidence.

Communicating risk: three framings

A percentile alone is not enough — it doesn’t say how much disease risk it explains [Kullo 2025].

Framing Example Caveat
Absolute risk “18% over 10 years” needs incidence data (often missing)
Relative risk / OR “2.3× population average” no baseline anchor
Percentile rank “top 5% of PRS” says nothing about absolute magnitude

Absolute risk linked to a guideline action is the most clinically actionable framing.

Integrating PRS into existing risk equations

  • Breast cancer — BOADICEA: the one clinical equation combining PRS + family history + rare variants + clinical factors
  • CHD — Pooled Cohort Equations: PRS is ~orthogonal → add log-additively
  • Most other diseases: no validated absolute-risk equation yet → estimate from epidemiological incidence
  • Lifetime risk can vary dramatically by PRS centile — e.g. ER-positive breast cancer ~2% to ~31% bottom vs top centile

The human barriers

  • Patients hold deterministic views of genetics; risk is actually probabilistic and modifiable (MI-GENES framed it as mutable)
  • Run many PRSs at once → most people flagged high-risk for something → alarm fatigue
  • Primary-care providers often lack genomics training → need CDS tools, a trained “champion user”, and PRS in medical curricula

PRS meets the electronic health record

Why the EHR changes the game

Biobanks now link genotypes to EHRs at population scale, so PRS can be built and applied without a bespoke study [Li 2020].

  • Khera et al. 2018: a PRS can flag people with risk equivalent to a monogenic mutation (CAD, AF, T2D, IBD, breast cancer)
  • Rich phenotypes: diagnoses, labs, imaging, meds — plus easy, well-defined controls
  • Examples: Michigan Genomics Initiative, UK Biobank, National Biobank of Korea, Biobank Japan, China Kadoorie

Turning an EHR into phenotypes

  • ICD codes — first-line case/control definitions (but coding practices differ between systems)
  • NLP on clinical notes — extract phenotypes from free text
  • PheKB — 50+ portable phenotyping algorithms with high positive predictive value
WarningEHR data is messy
  • Sparse & irregular — sicker patients have richer records (Geisinger: only 20/143 variables had <25% missingness)
  • Medication adherence not captured — prescribed ≠ taken
  • Phenotyping errors propagate into PRS evaluation

Infrastructure for clinical PRS

A workable pipeline needs more than a model [Kullo 2025]:

  • PGS Catalog — open repository of published scores (alleles + weights + metadata)
  • FHIR — standard for moving genomic + clinical data between systems
  • TRE / cloud — compute PRS on-demand with QC’d pipelines
  • CDS + EHR dashboard — show PRS alongside family history, smoking, labs
  • Metadata — record algorithm version + ancestry-specific performance for traceability

Beyond a single PRS: shared genetics

Genetic correlation — how much do two diseases share?

Genetic correlation (r_g) quantifies the overlap in heritable basis between two traits [van Rheenen 2019].

  • Bivariate LDSC — estimates r_g straight from summary statistics, robust to sample overlap (LD Hub hosts hundreds of traits)
  • Bivariate GREML — from individual genotypes
  • e.g. schizophrenia ↔︎ bipolar disorder r_g ≈ 0.6

A high r_g explains comorbidity and shared biology, and predicts cross-disorder risk in relatives — directly relevant when counselling families.

Why clinicians should care about r_g

  • Comorbidity — shared genetics anticipates co-occurring diagnoses
  • Borrowing power — pleiotropy-informed methods (MTAG) boost a small GWAS using a correlated, larger one
  • Cross-disorder risk — a relative’s risk depends on r_g, kinship, heritability and prevalence
Warning

r_g estimates can be distorted by assortative mating, misclassification, collider bias and stratification — interpret with the same care as MR [van Rheenen 2019].

Diversity & portability

PRS does not transfer across ancestries

  • Most GWAS (→ PRS) are European-ancestry
  • A European-trained PRS performs ~4–5× worse in African-ancestry individuals [Martin, in Li 2020]
  • Roots: different allele frequencies, LD, and effect sizes from distinct population history (drift, selection, bottlenecks) [Kullo 2025]
  • Deploying biased PRS clinically can widen health disparities

What to do about it

  • Prefer ancestry-matched base GWAS; use PRS-CSx / multi-ancestry meta-analysis
  • Report ancestry-specific performance and recalibrate per population
  • Invest in diverse cohorts — diversity also sharpens fine-mapping (W2)
ImportantFor Korean patients

Use Korean / East-Asian resources (KoGES, Korea Biobank Array “KCHIP”, National Biobank of Korea, TOPMed). Always check the base GWAS ancestry matches your target before trusting a PRS.

What a PRS cannot do

Honest limitations

  • Not causal — high PRS ≠ will develop disease
  • Misses rare, high-penetrance variants — BRCA1/2, Lynch syndrome need dedicated testing
  • Misses non-SNP variation — CNV/SV/repeats (W2 §Beyond SNPs)
  • Gene × environment — genetic risk is modifiable by lifestyle/medication
  • Not a diagnosis — one input among many, not a verdict
  • Dynamic — risk and methods both change over time

Hands-on

Dataset: CAD PRS from public summary stats

CAD GWAS summary statistics (e.g. Khera et al. 2018) + 1000 Genomes target genotypes.

library(bigsnpr); library(tidyverse); library(here)

obj.bigsnp <- snp_attach(here("data", "raw", "1kg_eur.rds"))
G   <- obj.bigsnp$genotypes
map <- obj.bigsnp$map

sumstats <- read_tsv(here("data", "raw", "cad_sumstats.tsv"))
glimpse(sumstats)   # SNP, chr, pos, a0, a1, beta, beta_se, n_eff, ...

Match & compute a C+T PRS

sumstats <- snp_match(sumstats, map)

ind  <- sumstats$`_NUM_ID_`
prs_scores <- big_prodVec(G, sumstats$beta, ind.col = ind)

prs_df <- obj.bigsnp$fam |> mutate(PRS = prs_scores)
summary(prs_df$PRS)

Visualize the distribution

ggplot(prs_df, aes(PRS, fill = factor(affection))) +
  geom_density(alpha = 0.6) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("#1D9E75", "#D85A30"),
                    labels = c("Control", "Case")) +
  labs(title = "PRS — CAD cases vs controls",
       x = "Polygenic Risk Score", fill = "Status") +
  theme_minimal()

prs_df <- prs_df |>
  mutate(prs_pct  = ntile(PRS, 100),
         top10    = prs_pct >= 90,
         bottom10 = prs_pct <= 10)

table(prs_df$top10, prs_df$affection)   # risk in top 10% vs rest

LDpred2-auto (more accurate)

corr <- readRDS(here("data", "processed", "ld_matrix.rds"))  # pre-computed

ldsc <- with(sumstats, snp_ldsc(ld_score, ld_size = nrow(G),
                                chi2 = (beta / beta_se)^2, sample_size = n_eff))

multi_auto <- snp_ldpred2_auto(corr, sumstats, h2_init = ldsc[["h2"]],
                               vec_p_init = seq_log(1e-4, 0.2, 30),
                               burn_in = 200, num_iter = 200)

beta_auto   <- sapply(multi_auto, function(a) a$beta_est)
prs_ldpred2 <- big_prodMat(G, beta_auto)

Save & document

prs_final <- prs_df |>
  select(FID, IID, PRS_CT = PRS) |>
  mutate(PRS_LDpred2 = rowMeans(prs_ldpred2))

write_tsv(prs_final, here("results", "tables", "prs_scores.tsv"))

renv::snapshot()   # reproducibility
sessionInfo()

Wrap-up

Key takeaways

  • PRS turns polygenicity into one actionable number — but it’s a risk indicator, not a diagnosis
  • Always evaluate incremental value, and don’t forget calibration
  • Clinical readiness = ACCE, not just AUC; utility evidence is still emerging
  • The hard parts are portability, communication, and EHR integration — not the maths
